newsitem.title: USA: Columbia to head home after new technical glitch.
newsitem.headline: Columbia to head home after new technical glitch.

text.p: NASA advanced the planned landing of the shuttle Columbia to Thursday morning after a navigation tool failed unexpectedly and forecasts called for worsening weather at all three shuttle landing sites, space agency officials said on Wednesday.

The decision to call the shuttle home 24 hours earlier came after one of the orbiter's three navigation units stopped working, and after a stuck airlock hatch last weekend forced NASA to cancel a pair of planned spacewalks. NASA engineers have been stumped by the hatch problem, which occurred for the first time in the shuttle's 15-year history.
The latest technical problem knocked out one of the shuttle's three crucial navigation units, known as inertial measurement units.
Although strict NASA safety rules ordinarily would force a shuttle with a navigation problem to cut short its mission immediately, Columbia is equipped with two back-up units, NASA said.
Astronauts were told to prepare for landing at the Kennedy Space Centre as early as 7:34 a.m. EST (1234 GMT) on Thursday, if the weather is clear and calm.

"We would like to land the shuttle tomorrow in Florida," said flight director Wayne Hale. "If the weather dictates otherwise, we have options at Edwards Air Force Base (in California) or we can stay up several more days."
NASA managers said forecasts called for rainy, unstable weather in central Florida on Friday, and windy conditions at two backup landing sites on the U.S. West Coast.

Although Hale said the "primary factor" for the shuttle's early return was the weather, he acknowledged the two equipment problems also played a role. "They certainly indicate that you ought to button things up and be prepared to come down at the earliest opportunity," he said, referring to the stuck hatch and the broken navigation unit.

A Thursday landing would be in line with NASA's original flight plan for the mission. Controllers earlier this week gave the crew the green light to remain in orbit an extra day to do more troubleshooting on the stuck hatch.
Earlier on Wednesday, astronauts aboard the Columbia guided the shuttle through a tricky manoeuvre to retrieve an orbiting telescope.

Through a series of precise rocket burns and careful steering, the five-member crew flew within 40 feet (12 metres) of the Orfeus-Spas, a powerful German-made space telescope. The telescope had been flying in formation with Columbia since the crew released it on Nov. 19, shortly after the shuttle was launched from Kennedy Space Centre.
Astronauts Tom Jones and Tammy Jernigan used the shuttle's robot arm to slowly pluck the satellite from space at 3:26 a.m. EST (0826 GMT) and tuck it into the payload bay for the ride home.

Scientists on the ground hope to collect data from the ultraviolet telescope to learn more about the life cycle of stars, especially the gaseous, soupy matter that acts as a nursery for stars outside the earth's solar system.

Preliminary data from the telescope showed it collected more information than had been hoped -- a total of 420 observations of nearly 150 objects in space, including Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the earth's moon.

"It's been an overwhelming and unqualified success," said Ronald Polidan, a member of the team of scientists directing the Orfeus-Spas work. "We have seen a number of different objects that did not look like what we expected."

The high resolution of the telescope will let astronomers see faint, faraway stars, examine the tenuous atmosphere that barely clings to the earth's moon, and learn how binary or twin stars exchange material.

In an unusually busy night for NASA, the astronauts reeled in the telescope just an hour after a separate team of space agency scientists successfully launched an unmanned Mars Pathfinder probe from Cape Canaveral. The probe is scheduled to land on Mars on July 4.
